key_takeaways: Insurers aren't bound by contractor bids, but must reasonably investigate and consider evidence.
Most gaps come from scope, pricing, repair-vs-replace, code, or matching differences.

body_html:
Your insurance company does not have to accept a contractor estimate, but it generally cannot ignore one either. Insurers must reasonably investigate a claim, so a detailed contractor estimate is evidence they should consider. If they disagree, they should explain why, and in Texas you can usually challenge the difference through supplements or appraisal.

Most claim disputes start with two very different numbers. Your roofer or general contractor walks the property and writes a repair price. The carrier's adjuster writes a lower estimate, sometimes far lower. When you send the contractor's number to the insurer, you may hear little back except that the company "stands by its estimate."

This article explains how insurers treat contractor estimates, the difference between ignoring and disagreeing, the most common reasons carriers reject contractor numbers, and what Texas property owners can do when the gap will not close.

What Role Does a Contractor Estimate Play in an Insurance Claim?

A contractor estimate is a written price to repair or replace damaged property based on what that contractor would actually charge to do the work. It reflects local labor, material costs, the contractor's overhead, and the scope they believe is needed.

Contractor estimates are valuable because they come from people who will actually perform the repair. They often catch items an adjuster missed, such as hidden water damage, code requirements, or manufacturer installation steps. They also serve as a real-world check on whether the insurance estimate can buy the repair.

They matter most when the damage is extensive, when hidden damage is likely, or when the insurer's scope looks generic.

How Insurance Companies Create Their Own Estimates

Carriers rarely use contractor bids as the basis for payment. Instead, their adjuster inspects the property and builds an estimate in software such as Xactimate or Symbility, using regional price lists for the property's ZIP code. You can read more in our guide to how Xactimate pricing works in Texas.

Software pricing is designed to represent typical local costs, but the estimate is only as good as the scope behind it. If the adjuster misses a line item, measures incorrectly, or chooses repair instead of replacement, the software will produce a lower number regardless of how accurate its pricing is.

Why the two estimates almost never match

DifferenceContractor estimateInsurance estimate
ScopeEverything the contractor believes is neededWhat the adjuster observed and judged covered
PricingContractor's actual price, including overheadSoftware unit costs for the ZIP code and month
Repair vs replaceOften full replacement for uniformityOften spot repair where possible
Code itemsIncluded when required to permit the jobMay be excluded or held pending proof
Hidden damageAllowances or discovery after tear-offUsually only what is visible at inspection

For a deeper comparison, see Xactimate vs contractor estimates.

Can Insurance Companies Legally Ignore Contractor Estimates?

The short answer: an insurer can disagree with a contractor estimate, but it should not simply ignore it.

Your policy promises to pay the covered amount of loss, not whatever a particular contractor charges. So the carrier is not bound to adopt your contractor's number. At the same time, Texas law expects insurers to handle claims fairly. Texas Insurance Code chapter 541 lists unfair settlement practices, including refusing to pay a claim without conducting a reasonable investigation and failing to attempt in good faith a prompt, fair settlement once liability is reasonably clear. You can read the statute on the Texas Legislature's statutes site.

This is general information, not legal advice. If you believe a carrier acted in bad faith, talk to a Texas attorney.

Ignoring versus disagreeing

  • Disagreeing looks like a reinspection, a written explanation of which items the insurer does not accept and why, or a revised estimate that addresses the contractor's points.
  • Ignoring looks like no response, a form letter that repeats the original number, or a refusal to look at new photos and documentation.

If you are getting the second response, put your request in writing, keep copies, and ask for a specific explanation of each disputed item.

Common Reasons Insurers Reject Contractor Estimates

  • Scope differences. The contractor includes items the adjuster did not see or did not consider storm-related.
  • Pricing disputes. The contractor's unit prices exceed the software price list.
  • Repair versus replacement. The carrier believes spot repairs will restore the property.
  • Code upgrades. Items required by current building codes may fall under limited or separate coverage. See ordinance and law coverage explained.
  • Matching and uniformity. The carrier refuses to pay to replace undamaged materials so new and old match. Our guide to matching issues in insurance claims covers this.
  • Lump-sum bids. A one-line bid with no quantities is easy for an adjuster to dismiss.
Tip: Ask your contractor for a line-item estimate with quantities, measurements, and unit prices. An itemized estimate is far harder to brush aside than a single total.

Red Flags That Your Claim May Be Undervalued

  • Several independent contractors arrive at similar numbers, all well above the insurer's estimate.
  • No contractor will do the job for the insurance amount.
  • Obvious items such as flashing, drip edge, underlayment, or detach and reset work are missing.
  • The estimate looks generic, with few photos and round measurements.
  • Hidden damage appears once work begins.

Our checklist of signs your insurance claim was underpaid covers more warning signs.

What Happens When a Contractor Finds Additional Damage?

Some of the biggest gaps between contractor and insurer estimates appear after work begins. Once a roofer tears off shingles or a restoration crew opens a wall, they may find rotted decking, wet insulation, damaged framing, or failed flashing that nobody could see during the original inspection.

This is normal, and most policies anticipate it. The insurer's first estimate reflects only what the adjuster could observe. When new covered damage is discovered, the right response is a supplement, not a fight over whether the original estimate was "wrong."

How to support a hidden-damage supplement

  • Stop and photograph the newly exposed damage before it is repaired or covered, with wide shots for context and close-ups for detail.
  • Measure the affected area, such as sheets of decking or linear feet of framing.
  • Explain the connection to the original loss, for example, water that entered through a storm-damaged roof.
  • Notify the insurer promptly and offer a chance to reinspect before the area is closed up.
  • Submit an itemized supplement rather than a change order with a lump-sum total.

Insurers are more likely to approve supplements that arrive quickly, with clear photos and a line-item breakdown. Waiting until the job is finished, with no visual record, makes it easy for the carrier to question whether the damage existed or was related to the claim.

How to Challenge an Insurance Estimate That Is Too Low

  1. Request a detailed explanation of every disputed line item in writing.
  2. Submit supporting documentation: photos, measurements, the contractor's itemized estimate, code citations, and manufacturer instructions.
  3. Request a reinspection with your contractor present.
  4. File a supplement for hidden damage discovered during repairs. See supplemental insurance claims explained.
  5. Consider appraisal if coverage is accepted but the amount is still disputed.

How Insurance Appraisal Resolves Competing Estimates

When the insurer accepts that the damage is covered but you cannot agree on the amount, the appraisal clause in most Texas policies offers a way out. Each side appoints an appraiser, and the two appraisers compare the estimates line by line. If they cannot agree, an umpire decides. An award signed by any two of the three is generally binding on the amount of loss.

Appraisers do not simply pick one estimate. They test each item: Is it needed to restore the property? Is it supported by evidence? Is the price reasonable for that market? A well-documented contractor estimate becomes strong evidence in that process, even though the contractor usually cannot serve as your appraiser. Learn more about our policyholder-side appraisal services.

What appraisers look at in competing estimates

  • Scope: whether each item is needed to restore the property to its pre-loss condition.
  • Quantities: whether measurements, waste, and counts are accurate.
  • Pricing: whether unit costs reflect the local market at the time of repair.
  • Causation and extent: whether disputed damage resulted from the covered event.

Because appraisal focuses on the amount of loss, it can move faster and cost less than a lawsuit. It does not decide coverage questions, which remain with the insurer and the courts.

Contractor Estimate Disputes in Texas

Texas property owners see contractor and insurer estimates diverge most often on hail-damaged roofs, wind-damaged siding and fences, and water losses. After a major storm in DFW, Austin, or Houston, demand pushes local labor and material prices up faster than software price lists may reflect, widening the gap between contractor bids and carrier estimates.

Texas also gives policyholders timing protections. Under the Prompt Payment of Claims Act (Insurance Code chapter 542), insurers generally must accept or reject a claim within 15 business days after receiving the information they requested, with limited extensions. Our Texas claim deadline calculator can help you track those dates.

Next Steps When Your Insurer Won't Consider Your Contractor's Estimate

  • Compare line items, not just totals, to see whether the gap is scope or price.
  • Get at least one more itemized estimate if possible.
  • Keep every letter, email, and call note.
  • Read your policy's appraisal clause and any deadlines.
  • Get an independent review before the dispute drags on.

faqs.q: Does my insurance company have to accept my contractor's estimate?
faqs.a: No. Your policy promises to pay the covered amount of loss, not a specific contractor's price. The insurer can write its own estimate and disagree with yours. However, it should consider the contractor's documentation as part of a reasonable investigation and explain the items it rejects. If the gap remains, supplements or appraisal are common next steps.

faqs.q: What should I do if my contractor's estimate is much higher than the insurance estimate?
faqs.a: Compare the two line by line to find whether the difference is scope, pricing, or repair versus replacement. Send the itemized contractor estimate with photos and measurements, request a written explanation and a reinspection, and keep records. If the insurer accepts coverage but still refuses to adjust the amount, consider invoking appraisal.

faqs.q: Can my contractor negotiate with my insurance company?
faqs.a: Contractors can share estimates, photos, and technical information, and they often attend reinspections. In Texas, though, negotiating a claim on a policyholder's behalf is generally reserved for licensed public adjusters and attorneys. Contractors who are not licensed should stick to explaining the repair scope rather than advocating for a settlement amount.

faqs.q: Why do insurance companies use Xactimate instead of contractor bids?
faqs.a: Software like Xactimate gives insurers a consistent, auditable way to price claims using regional cost data for each ZIP code. That consistency helps carriers handle large claim volumes. The trade-off is that the estimate depends on the adjuster's scope, and software unit prices may lag behind real market conditions after a major storm.
